title: Exceptions
cards/0/body: If a task faulted, await throws its exception, the very one thrown inside. You catch it with an ordinary try/catch around the await.
cards/1/title: An error before the first await
cards/1/body:
In an async method every exception goes into the task, even one thrown before the first await, for example by an argument check. It doesn't come out of the call itself; it shows up where the task is awaited.

An ordinary method that returns a Task without the async keyword would throw such an exception straight out of the call.
cards/2/options/2: Nowhere: the exception stays in the task, and await doesn't throw it
cards/2/explain: The method is marked async, so the exception from the check went into the task. The call returned an already faulted task, DoOtherWork ran, and await t threw the exception.
cards/3/body:
If you wait synchronously with .Result or .Wait(), the exception arrives wrapped in an AggregateException, with the original inside, in the InnerExceptions list.

Why the difference? .Result and .Wait() are APIs from .NET 4 (the TPL library), where a task can have several errors: for example, a task that waits for several others at once (next lesson). So they always throw a wrapper with a list. await was designed for code that looks synchronous: it throws the first exception from the list, with its original type and original stack trace (via ExceptionDispatchInfo).

GetAwaiter().GetResult() throws the original exception, like await, but still blocks the thread. It's the very method await calls under the hood (we'll take it apart in u3).
cards/4/q: Will this catch handle the network error?
cards/4/options/0: No: .Result throws AggregateException, with the HttpRequestException inside
cards/4/explain: One more reason not to block: the thread stands still, and exceptions arrive wrapped (and in a window, .Result also risks a permanent hang, u4).
cards/5/body:
If nobody awaits a task, nobody sees its exception. Since .NET 4.5 the app doesn't crash because of it; the error is simply lost.

The last chance to notice it is the TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException event. But it fires not when the error happens, but when the GC collects the task and its finalizer notices the unobserved exception. That may happen in seconds, in minutes, or never.

That's why "fire and forget" hides errors. The reliable way not to lose them is to catch them inside the task itself (more in u5).
cards/6/q: A faulted task was started and never awaited. When does TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException fire?
cards/6/options/0: When the GC collects the task: maybe in minutes, maybe never
cards/6/options/2: When the method that started the task returns
cards/6/explain: The unobserved exception is noticed by the task's finalizer, which runs only after a garbage collection. You can't rely on this event for logging.
cards/7/q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
cards/7/options/2: An exception before the first await in an async method is thrown at the await of its task, not at the call
cards/7/options/3: An exception from a task nobody awaited crashes the app immediately
cards/7/explain: With await, try/catch works just like with synchronous code. And since .NET 4.5 the error of a task nobody awaited doesn't crash the app; it is lost.
cards/8/pairs/2/1: The original, but the thread is blocked
cards/8/pairs/3/1: The error of a task nobody awaited
